study.title: ISLP Chapter 8: regression and classification trees
study.locator: Sections 8.1.1 and 8.1.2 (pp. 331 to 341): recursive binary splitting, Gini versus entropy similarity, and classification error reserved for pruning

focus: Split quality is the weighted child impurity \(G = (n_L/n) H(L) + (n_R/n) H(R)\). The parent impurity is the same for every candidate at a node, so minimizing \(G\) is the same as maximizing the impurity decrease.

sklearn tries midpoints between sorted distinct values with greedy exhaustive search, while Deep-ML 138 scores the raw values: the same four points yield threshold 3.0 under sklearn and 2.5 in problem 138.
Gini and entropy are numerically close and either works for growing; ISLP reserves the classification error rate for pruning toward accuracy.
ccp_alpha penalizes leaf count and prunes the weakest link first, which produces the nested candidate path that cross-validation then selects from.
units.reproduce: By hand on ordered labels A, B, A, A, A: parent Gini 0.32, split after the 2nd instance gives \((2/5) \times 0.5 + (3/5) \times 0 = 0.2\), split after the 1st gives 0.3. Then implement a midpoint scan with first-in-scan tie wins and match sklearn threshold 1.5 on X = [0, 1, 2, 3] with y = [0, 0, 1, 1] at max_depth = 1.
traps: Equal impurity does not mean a unique split. With two identical feature columns, sklearn picks feature 1 under seeds 0 and 1 but feature 0 under seed 42, so your scanner must define first-wins and test it.
A child can be less pure than its parent: the A, B child has Gini 0.5 against the parent 0.32. Only the weighted sum has to decrease.
HoML Chapter 5 never sets criterion, so every tree there is Gini. Request entropy explicitly, and remember the 138-versus-sklearn threshold convention before comparing answers.

selfTest.q: A node holds 3 positives and 1 negative. What are its Gini impurity and its entropy in bits?
Why does ISLP call the error rate weak for growing but prefer it for pruning?
selfTest.a: Growing needs sensitivity to purity shifts that leave the majority label unchanged. Pruning selects the final tree for accuracy, which is exactly what the error rate measures.

selfTest.q: The same data and code give different trees under a new random_state. Is that a bug?
selfTest.a: No. Tied splits can resolve differently across seeds, as the identical-feature test shows. Fix the seed for reproducibility and define your own deterministic tie rule.

selfTest.q: One leaf holds one vote for each of three classes. What does sklearn predict and with what probabilities?
selfTest.a: It predicts classes_[0], the lowest index, with probabilities \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1/3&1/3&1/3\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Argmax takes the first maximum.

units.why: Single trees have high variance: the same algorithm learns visibly different models from the same data. Bagging plus feature subsampling is the standard fix, and out-of-bag scoring gives a nearly free error estimate.

study.title: sklearn bagging meta-estimator
study.locator: 1.11.3 Bagging: bootstrap versus pasting, max_samples, max_features and oob_score

focus: A bootstrap covers about 63.2 percent of unique points since \((1 - 1/n)^n\) tends to \(1/e\). Each point is predicted by the trees that missed it. On make_moons(2000, noise 0.25, seed 0) with a 25 percent test split, 200 trees give OOB 0.934 against held-out 0.932.
Bagging helps unstable learners because averaging kills variance while bias stays put. Adding trees stabilizes the error; unlike boosting it has no residual-chasing loop to overfit with.
Forests force different top splits by sampling \(m\) near \(\sqrt{p}\) predictors per split, which decorrelates trees that would otherwise copy one strong predictor.
sklearn defaults differ by task: the regressor uses max_features 1.0, which is plain bagging, and ExtraTrees uses bootstrap False with random splits.
units.reproduce: Derive \(P(\text{missed}) = (1 - 1/n)^n\) tending to \(1/e\) near 0.368, simulate \(n = 1000\) to see about 63.4 percent unique, then fit RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, oob_score=True, random_state=0) on make_moons(n_samples=2000, noise=0.25, random_state=0) split with test_size=0.25 and random_state=0, and show OOB 0.934 against held-out 0.932.
traps: Treating OOB as free model selection. Each OOB prediction uses only about a third of the trees, so with few trees it reads pessimistic, and once you tune on it, it is no longer held out. Monitor with it; select with a validation split or cross-validation.
Soft voting needs predict_proba from every member. A default SVC in sklearn 1.9 has none, and the soft VotingClassifier still fits; the AttributeError appears only at predict time.
Assuming sqrt features for a regressor silently turns the forest into bagging. Read max_features per estimator instead of quoting the classifier rule.

selfTest.q: From \(n = 200\) points, how many land out of bag and how many trees predict each one?
selfTest.a: About \(0.368 \times 200 = 74\) points are missed per tree, and each point is predicted by the roughly \(B/3\) trees whose samples skipped it.

selfTest.q: Ten bagged trees give red probabilities 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.2, 0.55, 0.6, 0.6, 0.65, 0.7 and 0.75. What do majority vote and probability averaging predict?
selfTest.a: Majority vote says red with 6 of 10 above 0.5. Averaging gives 0.45 and says green. The combination rule changes the answer.

selfTest.q: Is a default RandomForestRegressor closer to a sqrt forest or to bagged trees?
selfTest.a: Bagged trees, because its max_features default is 1.0. The sqrt default applies to classifiers only.

selfTest.q: Why does raising \(B\) not overfit bagging while it can overfit boosting?
selfTest.a: Bagging averages fixed-complexity trees fit on resamples, so variance shrinks and bias holds. Boosting keeps fitting residuals, so late trees can chase noise; choose \(B\) by validation.

Implement stage-wise boosting around stumps, match sklearn on a toy, and diagnose noise sensitivity and overfitting by iteration count.
units.why: Boosting turns weak rules into strong models by fitting what is left over. The same loop powers the gradient boosting libraries, so its failure modes of noise chasing and late overfitting follow you into production.

study.title: ISLP Chapter 8: boosting regression trees
study.locator: Section 8.2.3 with Algorithm 8.2 and the three tuning parameters \(B\), shrinkage \(\lambda\) and interaction depth \(d\) (pp. 347 to 350)

study.title: sklearn AdaBoost usage
study.locator: 1.11.7 AdaBoost with 1.11.7.1 Usage: SAMME for classification, default decision stumps, and n_estimators with learning_rate as the main knobs

study.title: sklearn gradient boosting: loss, shrinkage and subsampling
study.locator: 1.11.1.2.5 Shrinkage via learning rate (learning_rate at or below 0.1 with large n_estimators) and 1.11.1.2.6 Subsampling (subsample 0.5, OOB pessimistic so prefer cross-validation)

focus: AdaBoost scores the round by the weighted error \(r\), pays the learner \(\alpha = \text{learning\_rate} \times \ln((1 - r)/r)\), multiplies wrong-point weights by \(\exp(\alpha)\) and renormalizes. The hand round gives \(r = 0.25\), \(\alpha = 0.5493\) and weights \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.2113&0.2113&0.366&0.2113\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), matching estimator_weights_.

Gradient boosting fits each tree to pseudo-residuals, the negative gradients of the loss. For squared loss those are ordinary residuals, and the target mean plus a depth-2 tree fit on the residuals exactly equals a one-tree GBM at learning rate 1.0.
Shrinkage, depth and count interact: small \(\lambda\) needs large \(B\) with typical values 0.01 or 0.001, depth-1 stumps give additive single-variable terms, and subsample 0.5 adds bagging noise.
Boosting uses no bootstrap and each tree depends on its predecessors, so \(B\) is a genuine overfitting knob. Choose it by validation or early stopping, unlike bagging counts.
units.reproduce: Run one AdaBoost round by hand on X = [0, 1, 2, 3] with y = [0, 1, 0, 1] and learning_rate 0.5: stump threshold 0.5 (2.5 ties; sklearn picks 0.5), \(r = 0.25\), \(\alpha = 0.5493\), new weights \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.2113&0.2113&0.366&0.2113\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Confirm \(\alpha\) against AdaBoostClassifier estimator_weights_. Then show GradientBoostingRegressor with learning_rate 1.0, one tree and max_depth 2 equals the target mean plus a depth-2 DecisionTreeRegressor fit on the residuals, on 50 points with \(x\) uniform on \([0, 4)\) and \(y = \sin(x)\) plus noise 0.05 at seed 0.
traps: Copying algorithm='SAMME' from the notebook raises TypeError in sklearn 1.9. The parameter is gone and discrete SAMME is the only behavior.
AdaBoost pushes weight exponentially onto mistakes, so mislabeled points attract ever more attention. Noisy labels hurt it more than they hurt bagging.
The learning_rate 1.0 residual demo is didactic. Real runs shrink to 0.1 or below with many more trees, or the residual fit jumps past good solutions.

selfTest.q: A stump has weighted error 0.25 with learning_rate 0.5. What learner weight does AdaBoost assign, and what happens to a wrong point starting at 0.25?
selfTest.a: \(\alpha = 0.5 \ln(3) = 0.5493\). The wrong point goes to \(0.25 \times \exp(0.5493) = 0.433\) before renormalization, which is 0.366 after.

selfTest.q: Why does boosting depth-1 stumps produce an additive model?
selfTest.a: Each stump splits on one variable, so each term is a function of one variable only. The sum over rounds is a sum of single-variable terms.

selfTest.q: A GBM with 5000 trees, learning_rate 0.5 and no validation set scores perfectly in training but poorly on new data. What broke and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Late trees overfit the residuals. Shrink the learning rate toward 0.1 or below, add row or column subsampling, and pick the iteration count by early stopping on validation.

selfTest.q: How does boosting reuse data differently from bagging?
selfTest.a: Bagging fits independent trees on bootstrap copies. Boosting refits the same data with modified weights or residuals, so each tree depends strongly on the ones before it.

focus: Learn the name map, in XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost order: step size is eta, learning_rate and learning_rate; rows are subsample, bagging_fraction and subsample; columns are colsample_bytree per tree, feature_fraction per tree and rsm per split (alias colsample_bylevel); L2 is lambda, lambda_l2 and l2_leaf_reg.

Defaults that bite: XGBoost eta 0.3 against LightGBM 0.1, CatBoost 1000 iterations with a rate it picks itself for the common losses, LightGBM bagging off until bagging_freq passes 0, LightGBM growing leaf-wise to num_leaves 31 with no depth limit (max_depth -1), and CatBoost symmetric trees at depth 6.

Early stopping differs per library: XGBoost takes early_stopping_rounds with eval_set and predicts from the best iteration, LightGBM takes early_stopping_round or the early_stopping callback with a validation set, CatBoost takes eval_set with use_best_model, and HGBT stops by itself only above 10000 rows.

Categorical handling differs too: CatBoost takes raw categories with ordered target statistics and one-hot encodes only features with at most one_hot_max_size values (2 by default), LightGBM takes integer-coded categorical_feature columns, and XGBoost takes pandas category columns with enable_categorical=True on the hist or approx tree method.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the 200-round learning-rate 0.05 depth-4 row and column 0.8 L2 1.0 early-stopped configuration for all four libraries, then correct every name and default against the docs. Run the HGBT version (max_iter 200, learning_rate 0.05, max_depth 4, l2_regularization 1.0, early_stopping=True, random_state 0) on make_moons(n_samples=2000, noise=0.25, random_state=0): it runs all 200 iterations because its internal validation score is still improving, and scores 0.955 on the data it was fit on (sklearn 1.9.1).
traps: num_leaves 31 with max_depth 4 cannot grow 31 leaves: depth caps the tree at 16 leaves, so set both consistently instead of copying the default.
bagging_fraction 0.8 alone changes nothing in LightGBM. Bagging stays off until bagging_freq is set above 0.
Copying n_estimators 100 into CatBoost without setting the learning rate silently swaps the shrinkage regime, since CatBoost defaults to 1000 iterations with an automatic rate.

selfTest.q: What are the default step sizes in XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost?
selfTest.a: XGBoost eta 0.3 and LightGBM learning_rate 0.1. CatBoost picks the rate automatically for Logloss, MultiClass and RMSE, from the iteration count, and uses 0.03 otherwise.

selfTest.q: Name the row-sampling parameter in each of the three libraries and any enabling switch.
selfTest.a: XGBoost subsample; LightGBM bagging_fraction, which needs bagging_freq above 0; CatBoost subsample, 0.8 under the default MVS bootstrap on CPU, while multiclass defaults to the Bayesian bootstrap.

selfTest.q: Should low-cardinality string columns be one-hot encoded for CatBoost?
selfTest.a: No. Pass them as categorical features and let ordered target statistics handle them; CatBoost one-hot encodes only features with at most one_hot_max_size values, 2 by default.

selfTest.q: When does sklearn HGBT stop early without an explicit validation set?
selfTest.a: With early_stopping auto, which is the default, it reserves validation internally on data above 10000 rows. Smaller data runs the full max_iter unless validation is passed.

units.title: k-nearest neighbors, search cost and the curse of dimensionality
outcomes: Implement brute-force kNN with uniform and distance weights and match sklearn predictions including a distance tie.
Explain how neighborhood size, weighting and feature scale move bias, variance and cost, and when trees lose to brute force.
Measure distance concentration and search time as dimension grows and state the scaling policy you would ship.
units.why: kNN is the purest similarity classifier: no training, all geometry. It punishes unscaled features and high dimensions faster than any other family, which makes it the ideal instrument for learning scale discipline.

next.note: Replace votes with margins on the same geometry.
Smooth the vote with RBF similarity.

study.locator: Sections 16.1 to 16.1.3 (pp. 547 to 550): the KNN decision rule, the curse of dimensionality with the growing-hypercube example, and k-d trees, hashing and approximate search for speed

study.title: sklearn neighbors: classification, regression and weights
study.locator: 1.6.2 Classification and 1.6.3 Regression: n_neighbors default 5, uniform versus distance weights, and the regressor averaging rule

study.title: sklearn neighbor search algorithms and cost
study.locator: 1.6.4 Nearest Neighbor Algorithms: brute force against K-D and ball trees, the auto-selection rule with leaf_size 30, and when high dimension or sparse input falls back to brute force

focus: The vote is a majority under uniform weights and an inverse-distance vote under distance weights. On the toy, query 2.5 has \(x = 0\) and \(x = 5\) tied for third place. sklearn warns that such ties depend on training order: in the given order \(x = 0\) joins, so uniform predicts 0 and distance weights give 1 at probability 0.652; reorder the rows and \(x = 5\) joins, so uniform predicts 1.

Scale is the model. With an informative feature on \([0, 1]\) (label \(x_0 > 0.5\)) and a nuisance feature on \([0, 1000]\), 5-NN scores 0.47 unscaled and 0.995 standardized (400 train and 200 test points, seed 0). Standardize inside a Pipeline so test data meets the same transform.

Distances concentrate fast: for 50 uniform points in the unit cube, the \((\text{max} - \text{min})/\text{min}\) ratio of pairwise distances falls from 101.9 at \(d = 2\) to 0.13 at \(d = 1000\), so fixed neighborhoods stop being local.

Trees win at low dimension and lose at high dimension. Timing fit plus 200 queries at \(k = 5\) on \(n = 20000\) uniform points: at \(d = 5\) ball tree takes 0.007 seconds against brute 0.02, while at \(d = 50\) brute takes 0.007 against KD 0.196 (one run on an i9-12900K, sklearn 1.9.1).
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement brute-force kNN with uniform and distance weights and match sklearn on X = [0, 1, 2, 5, 6] with y = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1] at query 2.5 and \(k = 3\). Make your tie rule explicit (lower training index wins), then reorder the training rows and show sklearn's uniform answer flip from 0 to 1. Rerun the scaling pair and report 0.47 unscaled against 0.995 standardized.
traps: Tuning \(k\) on train error always picks \(k = 1\). Memorization looks perfect and generalizes worst, so tune \(k\) by cross-validation.
Scaling before the split leaks test ranges into the train transform. Fit the scaler on train only and apply it to test.
algorithm auto is not a promise of trees. Sparse input, high dimension or \(k\) above half of \(n\) silently selects brute force, so confirm with timing rather than the parameter name.

selfTest.q: At query 2.5 with \(k = 3\), which third neighbor joins \(x = 2\) and \(x = 1\), and what does uniform voting predict?
selfTest.a: \(x = 0\) and \(x = 5\) tie at distance 2.5. In the given order sklearn takes \(x = 0\), so votes are 1, 0, 0 and uniform predicts 0; with the rows reordered it takes \(x = 5\) and predicts 1. A tie at the \(k\)-th place makes the answer depend on data order, so state your rule.

selfTest.q: Why does the unscaled toy score 0.47 while the standardized one scores 0.995?
selfTest.a: The nuisance feature spans 1000x the informative one, so Euclidean neighborhoods are chosen by noise. Standardizing restores the informative axis.

selfTest.q: The concentration ratio reads 101.9 at \(d = 2\) and 0.13 at \(d = 1000\). What breaks for kNN?
selfTest.a: Relative distance contrasts vanish, so the nearest and farthest points sit almost equally far. Fixed-\(k\) neighborhoods cover non-local regions and the vote carries little signal.

selfTest.q: At \(n = 20000\) and \(d = 50\), which search algorithm wins and why?
selfTest.a: Brute force at 0.007 seconds against 0.196 for KD-tree. Partitioning overhead and dimensionality defeat the trees while blocked matrix distance stays cheap.

study.title: ISLP lab: support vector classifier cost demo
study.locator: Support Vector Classifier: \(C\) 10 versus \(C\) 0.1 on the 2D example with wider margin and more support vectors at small \(C\), then grid search selecting \(C\) 1 at 0.74 CV accuracy

focus: The gutter constraints fix the margin width at \(2/\|w\|\). The toy gives \(w = 1\), \(b = 0\), width 2.0, support vectors at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\) with dual coefficients -0.5 and 0.5. Only points on or inside the margin enter the solution.

\(C\) is the violation budget. On negatives at -2, -1 and 2.4 and positives at 0.5, 1 and 2, \(C\) 0.05 gives width 9.756 with all 6 points as support vectors, while \(C\) 100 gives width 2.0 with 4. Train accuracy is 5 of 6 at both, because the point at 2.4 breaks linear separability.
Hinge loss is exactly 0 past the margin, so safe points vanish from the fit. Logistic loss never reaches 0, so every point keeps pulling, which is why only support vectors matter for the SVC.

Scale before fitting. With features on \([0, 1]\) and \([0, 100]\) and the label \(x_0 + x_1/100 > 1\), a default RBF SVC scores 0.75 unscaled against 0.97 standardized (200 train and 100 test points, seed 2). SVC defaults to RBF with gamma scale and \(C\) 1.0; LinearSVC defaults to squared_hinge and exposes no support vectors.
units.reproduce: Derive the width \(2/\|w\|\) from the plus-minus-1 gutter constraints. Solve X = [-2, -1, 1, 2] with y = [0, 0, 1, 1] by hand to w = 1, b = 0 with support vectors at -1 and 1, and confirm with SVC and kernel linear at large \(C\).
traps: Promising SVC probabilities from older tutorials now warns in sklearn 1.9 and disappears in 1.11. Never ship predict_proba without the calibrator wrapper.

Reusing a \(C\) value between SVC and LinearSVC. LinearSVC uses squared hinge and, through liblinear, also regularizes the intercept, so the same \(C\) gives a different model; compare decisions, not parameter values.
Skipping scaling is the classic SVM bug. \(\gamma\) and the margin both assume comparable units, and the mixed-scale example loses 22 points of accuracy without it.

selfTest.q: For \(w = [1]\) and \(b = 0\), what is the margin width and which toy points are support vectors?
selfTest.a: Width 2.0 with support vectors at \(x = -1\) and \(x = 1\), carrying dual coefficients -0.5 and 0.5.

selfTest.q: \(C\) 0.05 gives width 9.756 with 6 support vectors while \(C\) 100 gives width 2.0 with 4. Explain both changes.
selfTest.a: Small \(C\) tolerates violations, so the margin grows wide and every point sits on or inside it. Large \(C\) punishes violations, so the margin narrows onto 4 points.

selfTest.q: A 4-class problem goes to SVC. How many internal classifiers fit, and what does decision_function_shape ovr change?
selfTest.a: Six one-versus-one pairs fit inside libsvm. The ovr shape only reshapes the output scores, not the fits.

selfTest.q: A far-correct point contributes what to hinge versus logistic loss, and what follows for sparsity?
selfTest.a: Exactly 0 to hinge and a small positive amount to logistic. Hinge lets safe points drop out of the solution, leaving support vectors only.

study.title: ISLP lab: nonlinear support vector machines
study.locator: 9.6.2 Support Vector Machine: the radial kernel at \(\gamma\) 1 and \(C\) 1e5 overfitting, then the \(C\) and \(\gamma\) grid choosing \(C\) 1 and \(\gamma\) 0.5; 9.6.3 ROC Curves: the tuned model against \(\gamma\) 50 on training and test data

focus: The trick replaces every inner product with \(K\), so \(f(x)\) equals bias plus a sum of \(\alpha_i K(x, x_i)\) over support vectors only. The RBF form \(\exp(-\gamma \|x - z\|^2)\) makes far points contribute near zero, which is what locality means.

\(\gamma\) sets the ruler: large values spike the similarity and overfit, small values smooth everything toward underfit. The HoML grid crosses \(\gamma\) 0.1 with 5 against \(C\) 0.001 with 1000 to show both failures.
gamma scale equals 1 over (n_features times X.var()), verified exactly against sklearn internals. It is data-dependent, so rescaling silently retunes the kernel.

The Gram matrix holds \(n^2\) floats: 10000 rows in float64 need 763 MiB. Measured on the reference i9 CPU under sklearn 1.9.1, \(n = 1000\) takes 0.025 seconds and 7.6 MiB while \(n = 4000\) takes 0.171 seconds and 122.1 MiB.
units.reproduce: Hand-compute the Deep-ML 280 first test with \(\gamma\) 0.5: \(\exp(-4) = 0.0183\) and \(\exp(-1) = 0.3679\) give \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1.0&0.0183\\0.3679&0.3679\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Verify against pairwise.rbf_kernel, then time the Gram matrix at \(n = 1000\) and \(n = 4000\) and confirm the 16x memory step.
traps: sklearn \(\gamma\) is \(1/(2 \sigma^2)\), not \(\sigma\). Porting \(\sigma\) 0.5 from problem 21 means setting \(\gamma\) 2.0.
Kernel methods inherit the scaling requirement twice: distances and \(\gamma\) both assume comparable units.
Tiny \(\gamma\) makes every point similar to every other through a near-constant Gram matrix and underfits. Read the grid, never the default alone.

selfTest.q: Write the RBF matrix for \(X_1 = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) against \(X_2 = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) at \(\gamma\) 0.5.
selfTest.a: Squared distances are 0, 8, 2 and 2, so the matrix is \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1.0&0.0183\\0.3679&0.3679\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).

selfTest.q: How much memory does a float64 Gram matrix need at \(n = 10000\), and about how many rows fill 16 GiB?
selfTest.a: \(10000^2 \times 8\) bytes = 763 MiB. 16 GiB holds about 46000 rows, since \(46000^2 \times 8\) bytes is near 15.8 GiB.

selfTest.q: Same data, \(\gamma\) 5 versus \(\gamma\) 0.1. Which risks overfitting and why?
selfTest.a: \(\gamma\) 5: similarity decays within tiny radii, so each point predicts itself and noise becomes boundary. \(\gamma\) 0.1 smooths distant points together and risks underfitting.

selfTest.q: Why not expand RBF features explicitly instead of using the kernel?
selfTest.a: The RBF expansion is infinite-dimensional. The kernel evaluates that inner product in closed form from pairwise distances.

study.title: HoML Chapter 3: precision and recall tradeoff
study.locator: Book Chapter 3: The Precision/Recall Trade-Off (printed pp. 115-120). Notebook 03 cells: Precision/Recall Trade-off: retuning the decision threshold with precision_score and recall_score instead of trusting 0.5

focus: Impurity importance multiplies split impurity decrease by sample fraction, averages over trees and normalizes to 1. It is computed on train statistics and favors many-unique-value features, so treat it as a hypothesis, not a verdict.

Correlated features break both rankings. With \(x_0\) uniform, a near-copy \(x_1 = x_0\) plus 0.01 noise, a noise column and the label \(x_0 > 0.5\), a 200-tree forest splits impurity importance 0.498 and 0.498, while held-out permutation gives \(x_0\) 0.511 and \(x_1\) 0.0. Every tree needs an \(x_0\) split to finish the boundary, so \(x_0\) rescues points that a shuffled \(x_1\) misroutes but not the reverse. Yet \(x_1\) alone still scores 0.995: zero permutation importance does not mean useless.

class_weight balanced multiplies by \(n/(2 \times \text{class count})\), here \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.546&5.957\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) at 8.5 percent prevalence (two standard-normal features, label \(x_0 + x_1 + 0.5\,\text{noise} > 2\), \(n\) 4000, 30 percent test split, seed 0). Recall rises 0.64 to 0.95 while mean predicted probability doubles from 0.082 to 0.171 against a true rate of 0.086: weighting buys recall with miscalibration.
After weighting or resampling, 0.5 is no longer the neutral threshold. Retune it on held-out data or recalibrate before shipping decisions.
units.reproduce: Rerun the twin-plus-noise demo (2000 points, seed 0, 30 percent test split, 200 trees at seed 0) and report impurity \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.498&0.498&0.004\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) with permutation \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.511&0.0&0.0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) at spread 0.017 on held-out data; then drop \(x_0\) and show \(x_1\) alone scores 0.995. Rerun the 8.5-percent-prevalence logistic pair and report the recall gain with the doubled mean probability.
traps: feature_importances_ sums to 1.0, so ranks are relative: dropping a feature redistributes its mass and reshuffles the rest.
Permutation on train rewards overfit. Run it on held-out data with several repeats and report the spread, not just the mean.
Resampling to 50/50 then deciding at 0.5 exports the sampler prior. Keep original priors, recalibrate, or move the threshold explicitly.

selfTest.q: Twins read 0.498 and 0.498 in impurity but 0.511 and 0.0 in permutation. What happened?
selfTest.a: Trees split interchangeably on either twin, so impurity mass halves across them. The label is exactly \(x_0 > 0.5\), so every tree also needs an \(x_0\) split near the boundary: shuffling \(x_0\) breaks those splits, while \(x_0\) repairs anything a shuffled \(x_1\) misroutes. Permutation measures loss given the other features, not usefulness alone; \(x_1\) by itself scores 0.995.

selfTest.q: What multipliers does class_weight balanced assign at 8.5 percent prevalence, and from what formula?
selfTest.a: About \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}0.546&5.957\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) from \(\text{n\_samples}/(\text{n\_classes} \times \text{class count})\). The minority multiplier is roughly the inverse prevalence ratio.

selfTest.q: After weighting, mean predicted probability doubles while true prevalence stays fixed. Did accuracy necessarily improve, and what must change before deciding at 0.5?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. The weighted loss trades precision and calibration for recall, so accuracy can fall. Retune the threshold on held-out data or recalibrate the scores first.

selfTest.q: A noise feature reads 0.004 impurity against 0.0 permutation. Keep or drop it?
selfTest.a: Neither on one number: 0.004 of a normalized train-only score against exactly 0.0 held-out permutation says it contributes nothing measurable. Drop it only after the ablated model holds its score.
